title: JavaScript
intro: JavaScript makes pages interactive. Start with language basics, then learn the DOM, events, forms, storage, and fetching data — with live sandboxed demos.

topics.summary: A programming language that runs in the browser (and elsewhere) to add behavior.
topics.description: JavaScript can respond to clicks, change HTML, calculate values, store data, and talk to servers. Unlike HTML and CSS, it uses statements, variables, and logic to decide what happens next. In the browser it reaches the page through the DOM API. You will also see it on servers (Node.js), but this reference focuses on front-end use.
topics.whenToUse: Whenever a page needs behavior beyond static markup and styling.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not reach for JS to do what HTML or CSS already handle well (links, forms, simple layout).
commonMistakes: Treating JS as a substitute for semantic HTML.
Assuming code runs top-to-bottom across files without understanding load order.
beginnerTips: Learn HTML/CSS first so you know what JS is changing.
Open the browser console early — it is your main debugging tool.
topics.title: What JavaScript is

topics.summary: The browser parses and executes scripts, usually on a single main thread.
topics.description: The browser reads your script and runs it statement by statement on the main thread. A long-running loop can freeze clicks and scrolling until it finishes. Classic scripts without defer can block HTML parsing if placed in the head. Errors show up in the DevTools console with a stack trace pointing at the failing line.
topics.whenToUse: When deciding where to put scripts and how to debug runtime failures.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not micro-optimize load order before the page has real content and working behavior.
commonMistakes: Putting a heavy script in <head> without defer and wondering why the page feels stuck.
Ignoring console errors and guessing at the cause.
beginnerTips: Use defer or type="module" so HTML can parse without waiting on your script.
Reproduce bugs with console.log or breakpoints before rewriting large chunks.
topics.title: How JavaScript runs

topics.summary: Inline event attributes, <script> blocks, or external .js files.
topics.description: You can attach behavior with inline attributes like onclick, embed a <script> block in the page, or link an external .js file. External files (or ES modules) scale better: they cache, stay reusable, and keep markup clean. Inline handlers are fine for tiny demos but mix structure and behavior.
topics.whenToUse: When wiring behavior into a page for the first time.
topics.whenNotToUse: Avoid sprinkling onclick attributes across a growing project — prefer addEventListener in a script file.
commonMistakes: Copying large scripts inline into every HTML page.
Forgetting that inline handlers run in a different scope than modules.
beginnerTips: Start with one external file or module; split later when files get large.
Keep demo HTML simple so the JS lesson stays obvious.
topics.title: Adding JavaScript to HTML

topics.summary: Loads or contains JavaScript.
topics.description: The <script> tag either embeds code between its tags or loads a file via src. Classic scripts at the end of <body>, or with defer, wait until HTML is parsed. Modules (type="module") are deferred by default and support import/export. Async classic scripts download in parallel and may run as soon as they finish — order is not guaranteed.
topics.whenToUse: Whenever you need to load or embed JavaScript on a page.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not mix many competing load strategies (async + defer + modules) without a clear reason.
commonMistakes: Using src and inline code in the same <script> — the inline part is ignored.
Expecting async scripts to run in document order.
beginnerTips: Prefer defer or modules so the DOM exists before most of your code runs.
One module entry point that imports the rest keeps startup clear.
topics.title: <script>

topics.summary: Keep logic in .js files linked from HTML.
topics.description: External files separate behavior from markup. Browsers can cache them across pages, and version control diffs stay readable. This reference site loads ES modules from a js/ folder. Start with one entry file; import helpers as the project grows.
topics.whenToUse: Any real project beyond a one-off snippet.
topics.whenNotToUse: A single three-line demo can stay inline if linking a file adds noise.
commonMistakes: Duplicating the same script tag on every page instead of sharing one file.
Editing the wrong copy of a file because the HTML points elsewhere.
beginnerTips: Name files by feature (forms.js, nav.js) so you can find code quickly.
Match the script type to how you write imports — modules need type="module".
topics.title: External JavaScript files

topics.summary: // line comments and /* blocks */
topics.description: Comments document intent for humans; the engine ignores them. Use // for a single line and /* ... */ for longer notes. Prefer explaining why a choice was made, not restating what the next line of code already shows. Outdated comments are worse than none — update them when you change the logic.
topics.whenToUse: Clarifying non-obvious decisions, workarounds, or temporary TODOs.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not comment every line of obvious code; it adds noise.
commonMistakes: Leaving TODO comments that never get resolved.
Using comments to “disable” large blocks instead of deleting or branching cleanly.
beginnerTips: Comment the surprising parts: constraints, browser quirks, business rules.
Delete comments that no longer match the code.
topics.title: Comments

topics.summary: Instructions that perform actions; usually end with semicolons (ASI exists but be careful).
topics.description: A statement is one instruction: declare a variable, call a function, run a loop, or return a value. Most style guides end statements with semicolons even though Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI) sometimes inserts them for you. Expressions produce values; statements perform actions. Blocks { } group statements so they run together.
topics.whenToUse: Whenever you write executable JavaScript — almost everything is a statement or expression.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not rely on ASI edge cases; write clear statement boundaries.
commonMistakes: Omitting braces on multi-line if bodies and attaching the next line by accident.
Assuming ASI always does what you meant after return or throw.
beginnerTips: Read code top to bottom within a function; side effects happen in that order.
Use blocks with if/for so multi-line bodies stay unambiguous.
topics.title: Statements

topics.summary: Named containers for values.
topics.description: Variables give names to values so you can reuse and update them. Prefer const by default; switch to let when you must reassign. Avoid var in new code. Names should describe the value (totalPrice, isOpen), not cryptic abbreviations. Declare close to first use so scope stays obvious.
topics.whenToUse: Storing any value you need more than once or that will change over time.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not create variables you never read — that hides dead state.
commonMistakes: Using var out of habit and hitting hoisting/scope surprises.
Reassigning when a new const name would be clearer.
beginnerTips: const prevents reassignment bugs; it does not freeze object contents.
One idea per variable — avoid overloading a name with unrelated meanings.
topics.title: Variables

topics.summary: Block-scoped mutable binding.
topics.description: let declares a binding you can reassign later. It exists only inside the nearest { } block (or function) where it was declared. Unlike var, it is not function-scoped and is not usable before its declaration line (temporal dead zone). Use let for counters, flags, and values that change over time.
topics.whenToUse: When the same binding must point to a new value later (loops, accumulators, toggles).
topics.whenNotToUse: If the binding never reassigns, prefer const.
commonMistakes: Redeclaring the same let name in one scope.
Accessing a let before its declaration line.
beginnerTips: Declare the let in the smallest block that needs it.
Initialize when you can so the variable is never read undefined by accident.
topics.title: let

topics.summary: Block-scoped binding that cannot be reassigned.
topics.description: const creates a binding that cannot be pointed at a different value later. The contents of objects and arrays can still change — only the binding is fixed. Prefer const for most declarations; it signals “this name always refers to this thing.” Use it for config, DOM references you keep, and function definitions stored in variables.
topics.whenToUse: Default choice for almost every variable declaration.
topics.whenNotToUse: When you truly need to reassign the binding — then use let.
commonMistakes: Thinking const makes objects immutable.
Using const then fighting it with awkward workarounds instead of switching to let.
beginnerTips: const user = {}; user.name = "Ada" is allowed; user = {} is not.
Freeze objects with Object.freeze only when you need deep immutability guarantees.
topics.title: const

topics.summary: Legacy function-scoped declarations — avoid in modern code.
topics.description: var is the old way to declare variables. It is function-scoped (or global), not block-scoped, and declarations are hoisted so the name exists earlier than you might expect. That combination causes bugs with loops and conditionals. Modern code uses let and const instead.
topics.whenToUse: Reading or maintaining old code that already uses var.
topics.whenNotToUse: New code — prefer let/const.
commonMistakes: Declaring loop variables with var and sharing one binding across iterations.
Assuming var respects if/for block braces the way let does.
beginnerTips: When updating legacy files, replace var with let/const carefully and test block boundaries.
Know var exists so stack traces and tutorials do not confuse you.
topics.title: var

topics.summary: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, object, symbol, bigint.
topics.description: JavaScript values have types: strings for text, numbers for math, booleans for yes/no, plus null and undefined for emptiness. Objects (including arrays and functions) hold structured data. Symbol and BigInt appear less often at the start. The language is dynamically typed — one variable can hold different types over time, so check types when input is uncertain.
topics.whenToUse: Choosing how to represent data and debugging unexpected typeof results.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not over-engineer with custom type systems before you need them.
commonMistakes: Assuming a value is a number when a form gave you a string.
Using typeof to detect arrays (it returns "object").
beginnerTips: typeof null is "object" — a historic quirk; compare to null directly.
Use Array.isArray to tell arrays apart from plain objects.
topics.title: Data types

topics.summary: Text data in quotes ' ', " ", or backticks ` `.
topics.description: Strings hold text. Single and double quotes work the same; pick one style and stay consistent. Backtick template literals can span lines and embed ${expression} values. Many DOM APIs return or expect strings, so you will concatenate and format text often.
topics.whenToUse: Any human-readable text: labels, messages, URLs, JSON text.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not build HTML by concatenating untrusted strings into innerHTML.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that "10" + 1 becomes "101" because of string concatenation.
Mismatched quotes that break the rest of the file.
beginnerTips: Prefer template literals when mixing variables into text.
Trim user input before comparing or storing it.
topics.title: Strings

topics.summary: IEEE-754 floating point numbers (and BigInt for huge integers).
topics.description: Ordinary numbers are IEEE-754 floats, so fractions can be imprecise (0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3). Integers in a safe range still work fine for counters and most UI math. BigInt handles integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. Convert strings from inputs with Number(), parseInt, or unary plus — and check for NaN.
topics.whenToUse: Counts, prices (with care), sizes, timers, and calculations.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not use Number for money that needs exact decimal math without a dedicated approach.
commonMistakes: Dividing by zero without checking and getting Infinity.
parseInt("08") quirks — always pass a radix: parseInt(str, 10).
beginnerTips: Compare floats with a small epsilon when exact equality matters.
Number.isNaN(value) is safer than the global isNaN for type checks.
topics.title: Numbers

topics.summary: true and false — used in conditions.
topics.description: Booleans are the yes/no values true and false. Conditions, toggles, and flags use them constantly. Other values can be treated as truthy or falsy in if statements: 0, '', null, undefined, NaN, and false are falsy; most everything else is truthy. Prefer explicit comparisons when clarity matters.
topics.whenToUse: Flags, feature toggles, and any yes/no decision in code.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not store complex state as a single boolean when several cases exist — use clearer data.
commonMistakes: Writing if (x === true) when if (x) already expresses the intent for real booleans.
Treating the string "false" as falsy — non-empty strings are truthy.
beginnerTips: Name booleans like isOpen or hasError so reading if (isOpen) feels natural.
Boolean(value) or !!value forces a real true/false when you need one.
topics.title: Booleans

topics.summary: Intentional empty value.
topics.description: null means “this is empty on purpose.” You assign it when a value is known to be absent: no selected user, no result yet cleared. It is different from undefined, which usually means “never set.” APIs sometimes return null to signal “not found.” Compare with === null when that case matters.
topics.whenToUse: When you deliberately clear or mark a missing reference.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not mix null and undefined randomly in the same codebase — pick a convention.
commonMistakes: Using == null carelessly without knowing it also matches undefined.
Forgetting to null-check before reading properties (use optional chaining).
beginnerTips: Document whether your functions return null or undefined for “missing.”
nullish coalescing (??) treats only null and undefined as empty.
topics.title: null

topics.summary: A variable declared but not assigned, or missing return value.
topics.description: undefined appears when a variable was declared but never given a value, when you read a missing object property, or when a function returns nothing. It is the language’s default “no value” signal. Prefer initializing variables you will read, and return null or a real value when callers need a clear empty case.
topics.whenToUse: Recognizing default empty states from the language itself.
topics.whenNotToUse: Avoid assigning undefined manually when null better means “cleared.”
commonMistakes: Assuming a missing return is an error — many functions intentionally return undefined.
Confusing undefined with the string "undefined" from UI text.
beginnerTips: Parameters left out are undefined — give them defaults when useful.
Check typeof x === "undefined" only when the variable might be undeclared; otherwise compare to undefined.
topics.title: undefined

topics.description: Arithmetic operators perform math on numbers: add, subtract, multiply, divide, remainder (%), and exponent (**). The + operator also concatenates when either side is a string, which is a common source of bugs. Parentheses control order when expressions mix several operators.
topics.whenToUse: Any numeric calculation: totals, indexes, remainders, powers.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not use + to “add” numbers that are still strings from inputs — convert first.
commonMistakes: "5" - 1 works (4) but "5" + 1 becomes "51".
Integer division expectations — JS / always can produce floats.
beginnerTips: % is useful for wraparound (index % length) and even/odd checks.
Convert with Number(value) before math on form fields.
topics.title: Arithmetic operators

topics.summary: = += -= *= /= and more
topics.description: Assignment stores a value in a variable. Compound forms like += update in place: x += 2 means x = x + 2. The right-hand side is evaluated first, then stored. You can chain assignments, but clear one-step updates are easier to read.
topics.whenToUse: Updating counters, totals, and any stored state.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not overwrite const bindings — reassignment will throw.
commonMistakes: Writing = when you meant === in a condition.
Forgetting parentheses when mixing assignment with other operators.
beginnerTips: Prefer x += 1 over x++ when the value of the expression itself does not matter.
Keep assignments out of complex if conditions when it hurts clarity.
topics.title: Assignment operators

topics.description: Comparisons produce booleans used in if statements and filters. Prefer === and !== so both value and type must match — == coerces types and causes surprises ("0" == false). Ordering operators (<, >, <=, >=) work for numbers and for strings by lexicographic order.
topics.whenToUse: Branching, sorting checks, and validating ranges.
topics.whenNotToUse: Avoid == unless you intentionally want coercion and document why.
commonMistakes: Using == when === was intended.
Comparing floats with === after arithmetic without tolerance.
beginnerTips: Compare numbers to numbers and strings to strings — convert deliberately.
For nullish checks, value == null matches both null and undefined when that is desired.
topics.title: Comparison operators

topics.description: Logical operators combine or invert conditions. && returns the first falsy value (or the last if all truthy); || returns the first truthy. ! negates. Nullish coalescing ?? picks the right side only when the left is null or undefined — unlike ||, it keeps 0 and ''.
topics.whenToUse: Combining conditions and providing defaults.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not use || for defaults when 0 or '' are valid values — use ?? instead.
commonMistakes: Defaulting with || and wiping out legitimate 0 counts.
Writing if (a || b === 1) when you meant if (a === 1 || b === 1).
beginnerTips: Guard clauses: if (!user) return; keeps the main path flat.
Short-circuit && can replace a tiny if when the right side is a side effect — use sparingly.
topics.title: Logical operators

topics.summary: ++ and --
topics.description: ++ adds one to a number binding; -- subtracts one. Prefix (++n) updates then yields the new value; postfix (n++) yields the old value then updates. Many teams prefer n += 1 for clarity because prefix/postfix mistakes are easy in larger expressions.
topics.whenToUse: Counters in loops or simple tap tallies.
topics.whenNotToUse: Avoid ++ inside complex expressions where prefix vs postfix is unclear.
commonMistakes: Using the postfix result when you needed the updated value.
Trying to increment a const or a non-number.
beginnerTips: In for loops, the classic i++ form is widely understood.
Only use ++/-- on let bindings — const cannot reassign.
topics.title: Increment / decrement

topics.summary: condition ? ifTrue : ifFalse
topics.description: The ternary operator picks one of two expressions based on a condition. It is an expression, so it can sit on the right of an assignment or inside a template literal. Keep both branches short; nested ternaries become hard to read — switch to if/else.
topics.whenToUse: Simple two-way choices that produce a value.
topics.whenNotToUse: Multi-branch logic or long side effects — use if/else or switch.
commonMistakes: Nesting ternaries three levels deep.
Using a ternary only for side effects when an if would be clearer.
beginnerTips: Read it as “if condition, then A, else B.”
Wrap ternaries in parentheses when embedding them in larger expressions.
topics.title: Ternary operator

topics.summary: Run a block when a condition is true.
topics.description: An if statement evaluates a condition and runs the following block only when the result is truthy. Use braces even for one-liners so you can extend the block safely later. Keep conditions focused — extract a named boolean when the test grows complex.
topics.whenToUse: Any optional work that should happen only under a condition.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not use empty if bodies as placeholders — delete or finish the branch.
commonMistakes: Assigning with = inside the condition instead of comparing.
Relying on falsy coercion when only null/undefined should count.
beginnerTips: Prefer positive conditions when both forms are equal (if (isReady) over if (!isNotReady)).
Early return inside functions often replaces deep nesting.
topics.title: if

topics.summary: Alternative block when if was false.
topics.description: else runs when the matching if condition was falsy. Together they cover exactly two paths. Put the common or happy path first when it helps readers. If both branches assign the same variable, a ternary or early return can sometimes simplify the shape.
topics.whenToUse: When you need a clear fallback for the failing condition.
topics.whenNotToUse: Skip else when the if branch returns or exits — the rest of the function is already the other path.
commonMistakes: Duplicating large setup code in both branches — pull shared work out.
Forgetting braces and attaching else to the wrong if.
beginnerTips: Keep if and else blocks at similar length when possible for balance.
Name the condition so both branches read naturally.
topics.title: else

topics.summary: Chain additional conditions.
topics.description: else if adds another test when previous conditions failed. The first matching branch wins; later ones are skipped. Order matters: put more specific checks before broader ones. When many branches test the same value, switch may read better.
topics.whenToUse: Three or more mutually exclusive paths based on different tests.
topics.whenNotToUse: A long chain of equality checks on one value — consider switch or a map.
commonMistakes: Overlapping conditions where an earlier branch steals cases meant for a later one.
Forgetting that once one branch runs, the rest of the chain is ignored.
beginnerTips: End with a final else for an exhaustive fallback when every case needs handling.
Extract helper functions when each branch grows past a few lines.
topics.title: else if

topics.summary: Compare one value against many cases.
topics.description: switch compares one expression against case labels using ===. Each case should usually end with break (or return) so execution does not fall through. default handles unmatched values. Intentional fall-through is rare — comment it when you use it.
topics.whenToUse: Many discrete values of the same variable (status codes, modes, tabs).
topics.whenNotToUse: Range checks (score > 90) or unrelated conditions — use if/else if.
commonMistakes: Omitting break and accidentally running the next case.
Switching on a value that was never normalized (extra spaces, wrong type).
beginnerTips: Group cases that share a body: case "a": case "b": ...
Prefer returning from each case inside functions to avoid break noise.
topics.title: switch

topics.summary: Classic counted loop.
topics.description: A for loop runs a body while a counter condition stays true. The header has three parts: initialize, test, and update — typically let i = 0; i < n; i++. Use it when you need the index as well as a fixed number of repetitions. Keep the body short; call helpers for heavy work.
topics.whenToUse: Known repetition counts or index-based access into arrays.
topics.whenNotToUse: Simple array transforms — map/filter often read clearer.
commonMistakes: Off-by-one errors (i <= arr.length instead of i < arr.length).
Mutating the loop counter in confusing ways inside the body.
beginnerTips: Declare the counter with let so it is block-scoped to the loop.
Cache array.length in a local only if profiling shows it matters — readability first.
topics.title: for

topics.summary: Loop while a condition stays true.
topics.description: while checks the condition before each iteration. Use it when you do not know the count ahead of time — reading input until done, waiting for a flag, or draining a queue. Always update something that affects the condition, or you create an infinite loop that freezes the page.
topics.whenToUse: Repeating until a runtime condition changes.
topics.whenNotToUse: Fixed counts — a for loop states the intent more clearly.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to advance the state so the condition never becomes false.
Doing heavy DOM work every iteration without batching.
beginnerTips: Write the exit condition first, then fill the body.
Add a safety counter when talking to flaky external input.
topics.title: while

topics.summary: Runs at least once, then checks the condition.
topics.description: do…while executes the body once, then repeats while the condition stays true. Reach for it when the first pass must happen before you can decide whether to continue — rare in UI code, more common in “ask then validate” patterns. Prefer while when zero iterations should be allowed.
topics.whenToUse: When the body must run at least once before testing.
topics.whenNotToUse: Most UI loops — while or for…of are clearer defaults.
commonMistakes: Using do…while when zero iterations should be valid.
Copying a while body into do…while without revisiting the exit logic.
beginnerTips: Keep the condition identical in meaning to a while so readers are not surprised.
Still protect against infinite loops.
topics.title: do…while

topics.summary: Iterate values of iterable objects (arrays, strings).
topics.description: for…of walks the values of an iterable: arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, and more. You get each item directly without managing an index. Use entries() or a classic for when you need indexes. Prefer it over for…in for arrays.
topics.whenToUse: Reading each value in an array, string, or other iterable.
topics.whenNotToUse: When you need the numeric index on every step — use entries() or a for loop.

files.code:
const out=[]; for (const ch of "JS") out.push(ch);
document.getElementById("o").textContent=out.join(",");

commonMistakes: Using for…in on arrays and getting string keys plus inherited names.
Expecting for…of to deep-walk nested arrays without nesting loops.
beginnerTips: const item of list prevents accidental reassignment of the loop variable.
Break out early with break when you find what you need.
topics.title: for…of

topics.summary: Iterate enumerable keys of an object.
topics.description: for…in enumerates an object’s enumerable property names (keys), including inherited ones unless you filter. For arrays it yields indexes as strings and is usually the wrong tool — use for…of or array methods instead. Pair with Object.hasOwn (or hasOwnProperty) when you only want own keys.
topics.whenToUse: Inspecting keys on plain objects.
topics.whenNotToUse: Arrays and most modern object iteration — prefer Object.keys/values/entries or for…of.
commonMistakes: Using for…in on arrays for values.
Forgetting inherited properties from the prototype chain.
beginnerTips: Object.entries(obj) with for…of gives [key, value] pairs cleanly.
Remember key order for string keys is mostly insertion order in modern engines.
topics.title: for…in

topics.summary: Named reusable blocks of code.
topics.description: A function declaration defines a named block you can call later with arguments. Declarations are hoisted, so you can call them above their place in the file. Name functions after what they do (calculateTotal, not doStuff). Keep each function focused on one job so tests and reuse stay easy.
topics.whenToUse: Reusable behavior with a clear name and inputs/outputs.
topics.whenNotToUse: Tiny one-off logic used once may stay inline — extract when it clarifies.
commonMistakes: Giant functions that mix DOM, math, and networking.
Relying on hoisting then moving to const fn = () => and breaking call order.
beginnerTips: Prefer pure functions (same inputs → same outputs) when possible.
Put related helpers near the code that calls them.
topics.title: Function declarations

topics.summary: Parameters are placeholders; arguments are values you pass.
topics.description: Parameters are the names listed in the function definition; arguments are the values supplied at the call site. Extra arguments are ignored unless you collect them with rest (...args). Missing parameters become undefined — use default values (name = "Guest") when that helps. Pass only what the function needs.
topics.whenToUse: Designing function inputs and reading call sites.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not invent long parameter lists — group related data into an options object.
commonMistakes: Confusing parameter order at the call site.
Mutating object/array arguments and surprising the caller.
beginnerTips: Defaults apply only for undefined, not for null or ''.
Destructure an options object for readable named arguments.
topics.title: Parameters & arguments

topics.summary: Sends a value back to the caller and exits the function.
topics.description: return hands a value back to whoever called the function and stops further execution in that call. Without return, the result is undefined. You can return early to handle error cases first (guard clauses). A function can return any type, including other functions and promises.
topics.whenToUse: Whenever callers need a result — calculations, lookups, constructed nodes.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not return and also rely on sneaky global side effects as the main API.
commonMistakes: Writing return value on the next line without parentheses — ASI can insert a bare return.
Forgetting to return the result of a recursive or helper call.
beginnerTips: Return early on invalid input to keep the happy path unindented.
Be consistent: always return the same shape (or null) for a given function.
topics.title: return

topics.summary: Concise function syntax with lexical this.
topics.description: Arrow functions are a short syntax for functions: (n) => n * 2. They do not bind their own this; they inherit this from the surrounding scope, which helps in callbacks. They cannot be used as constructors. Single-expression bodies return implicitly; use { } and an explicit return for multi-line bodies.
topics.whenToUse: Short callbacks for map/filter and inline handlers that want lexical this.
topics.whenNotToUse: Object methods that need their own this — use a method declaration or function.
commonMistakes: Using an arrow as a prototype method and losing dynamic this.
Omitting parentheses wrongly for zero or multi-parameter forms.
beginnerTips: Wrap object literals in parentheses: () => ({ ok: true }).
Name arrows stored in const so stack traces and intent stay clear.
topics.title: Arrow functions

topics.summary: Where variables are visible.
topics.description: Scope rules decide which code can see a variable. let/const are block-scoped; function declarations create a function scope; modules have their own top-level scope; var and accidental globals pollute wider scopes. Inner scopes can read outer bindings (closures). Avoid globals — they collide and make testing harder.
topics.whenToUse: Reasoning about bugs where a variable is undefined or unexpectedly shared.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not invent deep nesting just to hide names — split functions instead.
commonMistakes: Creating globals by forgetting let/const/var in non-module scripts (sloppy mode).
Assuming a loop variable with var is unique per iteration.
beginnerTips: Closures remember variables from the outer function even after it returns.
Prefer modules over window.myApp globals.
topics.title: Scope

topics.summary: const list = [1, 2, 3]
topics.description: Arrays are ordered lists of values. The literal [1, 2, 3] is the usual way to create one. Elements can be mixed types, though consistent types are easier to work with. const list = [] still lets you push and change contents — only reassignment of list itself is blocked.
topics.whenToUse: Ordered collections: todos, search results, selected ids.
topics.whenNotToUse: Key/value records with named fields — use an object or Map.
commonMistakes: new Array(3) creates length 3 empty slots, not [3].
Confusing arrays with array-like objects (NodeList) — convert when you need map.
beginnerTips: Prefer [] over new Array(n) unless you intentionally want empty slots.
Array.from and [...iterable] copy or build from other iterables.
topics.title: Creating arrays

topics.summary: Zero-based access: arr[0]
topics.description: Array indexes start at 0: the first item is arr[0], the last is arr[arr.length - 1]. length is the count of elements (more precisely, one more than the highest index). Reading past the end yields undefined. Prefer.at(-1) for the last item when you want clearer intent.
topics.whenToUse: Reading or replacing a known position in a list.
topics.whenNotToUse: Searching by value — use includes, indexOf, or find.
commonMistakes: Using length as an index (off-by-one past the last item).
Assuming sparse arrays iterate the way dense ones do.
beginnerTips: Guard empty arrays before reading [0] if empty is possible.
length updates when you push/pop or assign beyond the end.
topics.title: Indexing

topics.summary: Assign to an index to replace a value.
topics.description: Assigning arr[i] = value replaces the element at that index. If i is beyond the current end, the array grows and may create empty holes. Prefer push/splice for adding, and immutable patterns (map) when you want a new array instead of mutating shared state.
topics.whenToUse: Updating an item you already located by index.
topics.whenNotToUse: Bulk transforms — map/filter express intent better than manual loops.
commonMistakes: Mutating an array that React/state or another module still treats as immutable.
Expanding length unintentionally with a huge index.
beginnerTips: Copy before mutating if other code still needs the old list: [...arr].
Check the index exists before writing when indexes come from user input.
topics.title: Changing elements

topics.summary: Add/remove at the end.
topics.description: push adds one or more items to the end and returns the new length. pop removes the last item and returns it (or undefined if empty). Together they treat the array as a stack. Prefer them over manual length fiddling.
topics.whenToUse: Stack-like behavior or appending to a growing list.
topics.whenNotToUse: Inserting at the start often — use unshift or better data structures for queues.
commonMistakes: Ignoring that push returns length, not the array.
pop on an empty array without checking.
beginnerTips: push can take multiple arguments: push(a, b, c).
Store pop’s return value when you need the removed item.
topics.title: push & pop

topics.summary: Remove/add at the beginning.
topics.description: unshift inserts at the start; shift removes the first element. Both reindex the rest of the array, so they can be slower on large lists than push/pop. Use them when order truly requires front operations, or consider a different structure for heavy queues.
topics.whenToUse: Occasional front insert/remove on small-to-medium arrays.
topics.whenNotToUse: High-frequency queue operations on huge arrays — cost adds up.
commonMistakes: Building a hot path that shifts thousands of items per frame.
Confusing shift (remove first) with pop (remove last).
beginnerTips: Document why you need front operations so future you does not “optimize” wrongly.
For queues, libraries or typed structures can outperform shift.
topics.title: shift & unshift

topics.summary: slice copies a portion; splice mutates by removing/inserting.
topics.description: slice(start, end) returns a shallow copy of a portion without changing the original (end is exclusive). splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) mutates: it removes and/or inserts at start and returns the removed items. Remember which one mutates before you share the array.
topics.whenToUse: Copying segments (slice) or editing in place (splice).
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not use splice when you wanted a non-mutating copy — use slice or toSpliced where available.
commonMistakes: Calling splice when you meant slice and deleting data.
Forgetting splice’s return value is the removed elements, not the array.
beginnerTips: arr.slice() copies the whole array shallowly.
Negative indexes count from the end in slice.
topics.title: slice & splice

topics.summary: Search for a value.
topics.description: includes(value) returns true/false if the value appears (using SameValueZero, so NaN is findable). indexOf(value) returns the first index or -1 if missing. Both use strict equality for ordinary values. For objects, they match by reference, not deep content.
topics.whenToUse: Membership checks and finding a primitive’s position.
topics.whenNotToUse: Finding by object fields — use find with a predicate.
commonMistakes: Expecting includes to deep-compare objects.
Forgetting indexOf returns -1, which is truthy if used carelessly as a condition.
beginnerTips: if (arr.includes(x)) reads clearer than indexOf !== -1.
Pass a fromIndex to skip earlier matches.
topics.title: includes & indexOf

topics.summary: Run a function for each item.
topics.description: forEach calls your function once per element with (item, index, array). It always returns undefined — it is for side effects, not building a new list. You cannot break early with break (use for…of or some). Prefer map/filter when the goal is a new array.
topics.whenToUse: Side effects per item: logging, appending DOM nodes, firing events.
topics.whenNotToUse: Transforming or filtering data — use map/filter/reduce.
commonMistakes: Expecting forEach to return a mapped array.
Trying to break out with return thinking it stops the loop — it only exits the callback.
beginnerTips: Keep the callback short; extract a named function if it grows.
async callbacks inside forEach do not await in order — use for…of with await.
topics.title: forEach

topics.summary: Transform each item into a new array.
topics.description: map builds a new array by running a function on every item. The original array is left alone. The callback should return the new value for that position. Chain map with filter when you need both transform and keep/drop — or combine carefully for performance on huge lists.
topics.whenToUse: One-to-one transforms: formatting rows, extracting fields, scaling numbers.
topics.whenNotToUse: Side effects only — use forEach or for…of.
commonMistakes: Using map but ignoring the returned array and mutating instead.
Forgetting to return inside a block-bodied arrow.
beginnerTips: Return a value from every branch of the callback.
map(item => item.prop) is a clean field extraction.
topics.title: map

topics.summary: Keep items that pass a test.
topics.description: filter returns a new array of items for which the callback returned a truthy value. The original is unchanged. Use it to narrow lists: active users, non-empty strings, scores above a threshold. Combine with map when you need both selection and reshaping.
topics.whenToUse: Selecting a subset without mutating the source.
topics.whenNotToUse: Finding a single item — use find. Checking existence — use some.
commonMistakes: Mutating the array inside the filter callback.
Using filter to pick one element and then taking [0] — find is clearer.
beginnerTips: Keep predicates named (isEven) when reused or non-obvious.
filter(Boolean) removes falsy values in a pinch — beware of keeping 0 if needed.
topics.title: filter

topics.summary: First item matching a test (or undefined).
topics.description: find returns the first element that satisfies the predicate, or undefined if none match. It stops searching once it succeeds. Use findIndex when you need the position instead. Ideal for “get the user with this id” style lookups on small-to-medium arrays.
topics.whenToUse: Locating one matching item by a condition.
topics.whenNotToUse: Collecting all matches — use filter. Simple value presence — use includes.
commonMistakes: Assuming find always returns an object — check before reading properties.
Using find for membership only and ignoring the value — some is enough.
beginnerTips: Handle undefined when no match is possible.
findLast exists when you need the last match in modern environments.
topics.title: find

topics.summary: some: any pass; every: all pass.
topics.description: some returns true if at least one element passes the test; every returns true only if all pass. Both short-circuit. Empty arrays: some → false, every → true. Use them for validation (“any invalid?”) and permissions checks.
topics.whenToUse: Boolean questions about a whole list.
topics.whenNotToUse: Gathering the matching items themselves — use filter.
commonMistakes: Forgetting every([]) is true and writing wrong validation for empty input.
Using map + includes chains when some would do.
beginnerTips: !arr.every(test) is “some fail”; !arr.some(test) is “none pass.”
Name predicates so some(isBroken) reads like English.
topics.title: some & every

topics.summary: Key/value pairs on an object.
topics.description: Objects store named properties: keys mapped to values. Create them with { name: "Ada" }. Read with dot notation when the key is a fixed identifier. Objects model records — a user, a settings bag, a config — rather than ordered lists.
topics.whenToUse: Grouping related fields under one value.
topics.whenNotToUse: Ordered sequences — use an array.
commonMistakes: Typo in a property name creating a silent undefined read.
Using objects as arbitrary string dictionaries when Map is clearer for dynamic keys.
beginnerTips: Keep property names consistent across the app (camelCase is common in JS).
const obj = {} still allows adding properties.
topics.title: Properties

topics.summary: Functions stored as object properties.
topics.description: A method is a function value on an object, usually called as obj.method(). Inside a regular function method, this typically refers to the object. Arrow functions as methods do not get their own this — they close over the outer this instead. Keep methods focused on that object’s behavior.
topics.whenToUse: Behavior that belongs with the data (format, save, validate).
topics.whenNotToUse: Standalone utilities with no object state — use plain functions.
commonMistakes: Passing obj.method as a bare callback and losing this — bind or wrap it.
Using an arrow for a method that needs dynamic this.
beginnerTips: Shorthand: const obj = { greet() { return "hi"; } }.
Extract methods that do not use this into module-level functions.
topics.title: Methods

topics.summary: obj.key vs obj["key"]
topics.description: Dot access (obj.key) is concise for fixed identifiers. Bracket access (obj["key"] or obj[name]) is required for dynamic keys, keys with spaces, or keys that are not valid identifiers. Missing properties read as undefined. Optional chaining obj?.key stops safely when obj is nullish.
topics.whenToUse: Reading and writing fields — brackets when the key is computed.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not use brackets for every access; dots read better for known names.
commonMistakes: obj[key] vs obj.key confusion when key is a variable.
Writing obj."name" which is a syntax error — use brackets.
beginnerTips: const key = "name"; user[key] reads a dynamic field.
Combine with nullish coalescing: user.nickname ?? user.name.
topics.title: Object access

topics.summary: Objects inside objects.
topics.description: Objects often nest: user.address.city. Dig in carefully — a missing middle level throws if you read .city on undefined. Optional chaining (user.address?.city) and nullish defaults keep reads safe. Avoid deep nesting when a flatter shape would do.
topics.whenToUse: Hierarchical data from APIs or forms with grouped fields.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not nest five levels for convenience — normalize data when it hurts.
commonMistakes: Assuming every nested path exists after a partial JSON response.
Mutating nested objects that other parts of the app still reference.
beginnerTips: Update nested fields immutably when sharing state: { ...user, address: { ...user.address, city } }.
Validate API shapes before deep access.
topics.title: Nested objects

topics.summary: Common data shape for lists of records.
topics.description: Most app lists are arrays of objects: [{ id, title }, …]. You map for display, filter for search, and find by id. Keep a stable unique id on each record. When updating one item, build a new array with map so you do not mutate shared state by accident.
topics.whenToUse: Tables, cards, search results, and any list of records.
topics.whenNotToUse: A single record — use one object, not a one-item array, unless the API requires it.
commonMistakes: Using index as a React key when ids exist and order can change.
find by name when names are not unique — use id.
beginnerTips: Normalize once: array for order, Map by id for fast lookup if needed.
JSON from APIs often arrives in this shape — practice map/filter on it.
topics.title: Arrays of objects

topics.summary: Unpack values from objects/arrays into variables.
topics.description: Destructuring copies properties or array positions into local variables: const { name } = user; const [first, second] = list. You can rename ({ name: userName }), set defaults, and nest. It shortens repetitive access and clarifies which fields a function needs.
topics.whenToUse: Pulling a few fields out of objects/arrays at the start of a block or parameter list.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not destructure huge objects just to use one field once — a single read is fine.
commonMistakes: Destructuring undefined/null — throws; default the object first.
Mixing up array order when the API fields are named — prefer object destructuring.
beginnerTips: Function params: function greet({ name }) { ... } documents the expected shape.
Rest: const { id, ...rest } = row keeps leftover fields.
topics.title: Destructuring
topics.syntax:
const { name } = user;
const [first, second] = list;

subsections.title: DOM
subsections.description: The Document Object Model — JavaScript’s view of the page.

topics.summary: The entry object representing the page.
topics.description: document is the root object for the current page’s DOM. From it you query elements, create nodes, and listen for document-wide events. Most browser page APIs hang off document or off elements you find through it. In modules, wait until the DOM is ready (or place scripts with defer) before querying.
topics.whenToUse: Any script that reads or changes page structure.
topics.whenNotToUse: Server-side Node code has no browser document unless you use a library.
commonMistakes: Querying elements before they exist in the DOM.
Confusing document with window — they are related but different objects.
beginnerTips: document.documentElement is <html>; document.body is <body>.
Prefer document methods over obsolete aliases.
topics.title: document

topics.summary: Find one element by its unique id.
topics.description: getElementById looks up a single element whose id attribute matches. Ids must be unique in the document. It returns the element or null if missing — always check before using. It is fast and clear for known landmark nodes like #app or #output.
topics.whenToUse: Targeting one unique element you control in the HTML.
topics.whenNotToUse: Selecting by class or complex structure — use querySelector.
commonMistakes: Calling getElementById without document.
Assuming it never returns null.
beginnerTips: Store the result in a const if you use it more than once.
Id selectors in CSS/querySelector use #id — getElementById takes the bare name.
topics.title: getElementById

topics.summary: Find the first element matching a CSS selector.
topics.description: querySelector returns the first element that matches a CSS selector string, or null. You can use classes, attributes, combinators — anything CSS supports. Scope the search with element.querySelector to search only under a parent. For all matches, use querySelectorAll.
topics.whenToUse: Flexible lookups when id is not enough.
topics.whenNotToUse: Hot loops selecting the same node — cache the result.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the leading . for classes or # for ids.
Using querySelector when you needed every match.
beginnerTips: Prefer specific selectors under a known root to avoid grabbing the wrong node.
Escape special characters in selectors when ids/classes are dynamic.
topics.title: querySelector

topics.summary: Find all matching elements (NodeList).
topics.description: querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList of all matches for a selector. It has forEach; convert with [...list] or Array.from when you need map/filter. Unlike live HTMLCollections, it does not auto-update when the DOM changes. Iterate and update each node deliberately.
topics.whenToUse: Applying the same change to every matching element.
topics.whenNotToUse: A single element — querySelector is enough.
commonMistakes: Expecting the NodeList to grow when you add new matching elements later.
Calling map directly on the NodeList in older environments without converting.
beginnerTips: Cache the NodeList if the selector is expensive and the DOM is stable.
Combine with closest in event delegation patterns.
topics.title: querySelectorAll

topics.summary: Live HTMLCollection by class name.
topics.description: getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection of elements with a given class. Live means it updates as the DOM changes. Modern code often prefers querySelectorAll(".name") for consistency with CSS selectors and a static snapshot. Still useful to recognize in older examples.
topics.whenToUse: Working with legacy code that already uses it.
topics.whenNotToUse: New code — prefer querySelectorAll for clearer selectors.
commonMistakes: Treating the collection like a full Array without converting.
Modifying the DOM while iterating a live collection and skipping elements.
beginnerTips: Live collections can surprise you while looping and removing nodes.
Class names are space-separated lists — the method matches tokens.
topics.title: getElementsByClassName

topics.summary: Live collection by tag name.
topics.description: getElementsByTagName returns a live HTMLCollection of elements with that tag ("p", "div", "*"). Like other live collections, it reflects DOM changes. Prefer querySelectorAll("p") in new code unless you specifically want a live list of tags.
topics.whenToUse: Legacy patterns or quickly listing all tags of one type.
topics.whenNotToUse: Complex matching — CSS selectors via querySelectorAll are more expressive.
commonMistakes: Assuming the collection is a static array snapshot.
Using tagName checks incorrectly — element.tagName is usually uppercase in HTML.
beginnerTips: document.getElementsByTagName("div") searches the whole document.
Call it on an element to search only descendants.
topics.title: getElementsByTagName

topics.summary: Get/set plain text (safe from HTML injection).
topics.description: textContent gets or sets the plain text inside an element. Tags in the string are shown as text, not parsed as HTML, which avoids injection bugs. Prefer it for user-provided strings and simple labels. It overwrites all descendants’ text content when set.
topics.whenToUse: Displaying or updating readable text safely.
topics.whenNotToUse: When you must insert real HTML elements — build nodes or use carefully sanitized HTML.
commonMistakes: Using innerHTML for plain text and opening XSS holes.
Expecting HTML entities in the string to render as markup.
beginnerTips: Reading textContent concatenates text from descendants.
Use it to clear an element: el.textContent = "".
topics.title: textContent

topics.summary: Get/set HTML markup inside an element.
topics.description: innerHTML reads or writes HTML markup as a string. The browser parses the string into real elements. Never assign unsanitized user input — that is a classic XSS path. Prefer textContent, createElement, or a vetted sanitizer when content is untrusted.
topics.whenToUse: Trusted static markup snippets you control.
topics.whenNotToUse: Any string that includes user or third-party input without sanitizing.
commonMistakes: Inserting unsanitized user input via innerHTML.
Building large UIs with repeated innerHTML string concatenation.
beginnerTips: Setting innerHTML replaces all children — save nodes you still need first.
For single elements, createElement + append is often clearer and safer.
topics.title: innerHTML

topics.summary: getAttribute / setAttribute / element.id / element.href
topics.description: Attributes describe HTML properties on elements. Use getAttribute/setAttribute for arbitrary names, or properties like element.id and element.href for common ones. Boolean attributes (disabled, checked) are often easier via element.disabled = true. Reflect changes carefully — some properties normalize values (URLs on href).
topics.whenToUse: Reading or updating HTML attributes from script.
topics.whenNotToUse: Styling — prefer classes; do not set style attributes for every UI state.
commonMistakes: Confusing getAttribute("checked") with the live checked property on inputs.
Setting class via setAttribute and fighting classList elsewhere.
beginnerTips: data-* attributes pair with element.dataset for custom metadata.
removeAttribute clears an attribute entirely.
topics.title: Attributes

topics.summary: Prefer classList over className string surgery.
topics.description: CSS classes are the main way JS should switch visual states. classList.add/remove/toggle/contains avoid brittle string edits on className. Keep styling in CSS; let JS only flip class names that your stylesheet understands. See classList topics for details.
topics.whenToUse: Toggling UI states: open/closed, active, theme, error.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not encode complex style values in class names when a CSS variable or data attribute fits better.
commonMistakes: Rebuilding the entire className string and wiping unrelated classes.
Setting element.style for everything instead of reusable classes.
beginnerTips: Name state classes clearly: is-open, has-error.
One responsibility per class keeps CSS predictable.
topics.title: Classes via JS

topics.summary: element.style.color = 'red' sets inline styles.
topics.description: element.style sets inline styles that override most stylesheet rules for those properties. Use camelCase property names in JS (backgroundColor). Prefer CSS classes for ongoing UI states so designers can tweak visuals without hunting through scripts. Inline styles are fine for one-off computed values (width from measurement).
topics.whenToUse: Dynamic values you cannot know ahead of time in CSS.
topics.whenNotToUse: Theme and state styling that belongs in a stylesheet.
commonMistakes: Fighting !important and specificity wars with inline styles everywhere.
Using kebab-case el.style["background-color"] inconsistently — camelCase is the norm.
beginnerTips: el.style.setProperty("--x", value) updates CSS variables.
Clear an inline style with el.style.color = "".
topics.title: Styles via JS

topics.summary: document.createElement('button') builds a new element.
topics.description: createElement makes a new element node that is not yet on the page. Set text, attributes, listeners, then insert it with append/appendChild. Building nodes this way avoids innerHTML injection risks and keeps structure explicit. Create the right tag for the job (button vs a vs div).
topics.whenToUse: Constructing UI pieces from data or user actions.
topics.whenNotToUse: Static content that belongs in the HTML file from the start.
commonMistakes: Creating elements and forgetting to append them.
Using <div> with a click handler instead of <button> for actions.
beginnerTips: Set classList and attributes before appending to reduce reflows in tight loops.
Use DocumentFragment when inserting many siblings at once.
topics.title: createElement

topics.summary: Append a node as the last child.
topics.description: appendChild adds a node as the last child of a parent and returns the child. If the node was already in the DOM, it is moved — not copied. Prefer parent.append(...nodes) when you want to add multiple nodes or strings more conveniently.
topics.whenToUse: Inserting a single node at the end of a parent.
topics.whenNotToUse: Inserting at a specific position — use before/after or insertBefore.
commonMistakes: Appending a string with appendChild — it needs a text node or use append.
Losing existing children unexpectedly when replacing via innerHTML instead.
beginnerTips: Moving a node with appendChild reparents it automatically.
Learn append, prepend, and remove for modern brevity.
topics.title: appendChild

topics.summary: append, prepend, replaceWith, remove, before, after
topics.description: Modern DOM methods reduce boilerplate: append/prepend accept multiple nodes and strings; before/after insert siblings; replaceWith swaps a node; remove drops it without needing parentNode. They make dynamic UI code shorter and clearer than older insertBefore patterns.
topics.whenToUse: Everyday DOM surgery in modern browsers.
topics.whenNotToUse: Very old browser targets without polyfills — check your support matrix.
commonMistakes: Calling remove on a node you still hold and assuming it is destroyed for GC immediately while listeners linger.
Mixing old and new APIs inconsistently in the same module.
beginnerTips: el.remove() is clearer than el.parentNode.removeChild(el).
replaceWith can take multiple nodes as replacements.
topics.title: Modern alternatives

topics.summary: Compose interfaces from data using createElement loops.
topics.description: Dynamic UI means turning data into elements at runtime: map an array to list items, render search results, or rebuild a menu. Clear the host (textContent = "") or reuse a template pattern, then append new nodes. Keep rendering functions pure when you can: data in, DOM out.
topics.whenToUse: Lists and views driven by arrays/objects from memory or APIs.
topics.whenNotToUse: Fully static pages — write the HTML directly.
commonMistakes: Concatenating untrusted HTML strings instead of textContent on each node.
Leaving duplicate listeners by re-rendering without cleaning up.
beginnerTips: Extract a renderItem(data) helper so the loop stays thin.
Avoid rebuilding the entire tree on every keystroke if only one label changed.
topics.title: Building UI dynamically

topics.summary: Register a function to run when an event occurs.
topics.description: addEventListener(type, handler) runs your function when that event fires on the element. You can attach multiple listeners for the same type. Pass the same function reference to removeEventListener when cleaning up. Prefer this over inline onclick attributes in real projects.
topics.whenToUse: Responding to user or browser events on elements or window/document.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not stack duplicate listeners on every render without removing old ones.
commonMistakes: Adding an anonymous function and then being unable to remove it.
Listening on null because the element was not found.
beginnerTips: Use { once: true } for one-shot handlers.
Delegation: listen on a parent and inspect event.target for dynamic children.
topics.title: addEventListener

topics.summary: Primary activation event for buttons and similar controls.
topics.description: The click event fires on primary activation — mouse click, and in many cases keyboard activation on buttons/links. Use it for actions: submit via JS, toggle panels, navigate in single-page apps. Prefer real <button> elements so keyboard users get the same behavior for free.
topics.whenToUse: Button actions and clickable controls.
topics.whenNotToUse: Page navigation — prefer <a href> unless you intercept carefully.
commonMistakes: Putting click handlers on non-interactive divs without keyboard support.
Using click for every keystroke-like update — use input for fields.
beginnerTips: event.preventDefault() stops default button/link behavior when needed.
Distinguish click from dblclick; do not rely on double-click for essential actions.
topics.title: click

topics.summary: mouseover, mouseout, mousemove, contextmenu…
topics.description: Mouse events report pointer movement and buttons: mouseover/mouseout, mousemove, contextmenu (right-click), and more. They can fire often — keep mousemove handlers light. Pointer events (pointerdown, etc.) unify mouse, touch, and pen in modern apps.
topics.whenToUse: Hover effects beyond CSS, drag interactions, custom context menus.
topics.whenNotToUse: Simple hover styling — use CSS :hover instead.
commonMistakes: Doing heavy work on every mousemove.
Breaking mobile by assuming a mouse always exists.
beginnerTips: mouseenter/mouseleave do not bubble the same way as mouseover/mouseout — pick intentionally.
Prefer pointer events for new cross-input code.
topics.title: Mouse events

topics.summary: keydown, keyup — inspect event.key
topics.description: Keyboard events fire when keys are pressed or released. Prefer event.key ("Enter", "a", "Escape") over legacy keyCode. keydown repeats while held; keyup fires once on release. Listen on the focused element or document/window for global shortcuts — and do not override assistive or browser shortcuts carelessly.
topics.whenToUse: Shortcuts, game controls, Enter-to-submit enhancements.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not trap focus or steal keys needed by screen readers and the browser.
commonMistakes: Relying on keyCode numbers from old tutorials.
Attaching shortcuts that conflict with browser find or refresh.
beginnerTips: Check event.ctrlKey / metaKey / shiftKey for combos.
Use keydown for Escape-to-close patterns.
topics.title: Keyboard events

topics.summary: input fires on most value edits; change fires on commit.
topics.description: The input event fires as the user edits (each keystroke for text fields). change fires when the edit is committed — often on blur for text, or immediately for checkboxes/selects. Use input for live previews and change for finalized values. Read the value from event.target.value.
topics.whenToUse: Reacting to field edits and selection changes.
topics.whenNotToUse: Button presses — use click. Form send — use submit.
commonMistakes: Listening for keyup only and missing paste/autofill — input covers those.
Forgetting that some inputs fire change differently across controls.
beginnerTips: Debounce expensive live search on input events.
change is enough when you only care after the user leaves the field.
topics.title: input & change

topics.summary: Form submission event — preventDefault to handle with JS.
topics.description: submit fires on the form when the user sends it (button, Enter). Call event.preventDefault() to stop the browser’s navigation/reload and handle data with JS instead. Listen on the <form>, not only the button, so every submit path is covered. Read fields with FormData or direct .value access.
topics.whenToUse: Custom form handling, client checks, or fetch-based saves.
topics.whenNotToUse: When a full page POST/GET is desired — let the browser submit normally.
commonMistakes: Binding only the button click and missing Enter-key submits.
Forgetting preventDefault and losing in-memory state on reload.
beginnerTips: Disable the submit button while a request is in flight to prevent doubles.
Include name attributes so FormData picks fields up.
topics.title: submit

topics.summary: DOMContentLoaded: HTML parsed; load: everything including images.
topics.description: DOMContentLoaded fires when HTML is parsed and defer/module scripts have run — images may still be loading. load on window fires when the full page and resources finish. Modules already wait for parsing before executing, so you often do not need DOMContentLoaded inside them. Use load for measurements that need final layout/images.
topics.whenToUse: Running code at the right readiness milestone.
topics.whenNotToUse: Unnecessary wrapping of module code that already runs after parse.
commonMistakes: Waiting for full load before enabling basic interactivity.
Attaching DOMContentLoaded after it already fired and never running setup.
beginnerTips: document.readyState can tell you if you already missed the event.
Prefer defer/module placement over racing DOMContentLoaded.
topics.title: load & DOMContentLoaded

topics.summary: Handlers receive an event describing what happened.
topics.description: Every listener receives an event object: what fired, on which element, and helpers to control behavior. Useful fields include target (origin), currentTarget (the element with the listener), key for keyboard events, and methods preventDefault and stopPropagation. Read what you need; ignore the rest.
topics.whenToUse: Any non-trivial handler — inspection and default control live here.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not stopPropagation everywhere; it breaks other listeners and analytics.
commonMistakes: Confusing target with currentTarget during bubbling.
Calling preventDefault too late after async work — it must be synchronous in the handler.
beginnerTips: prefer event.target.closest("selector") in delegated handlers.
Type narrow in TypeScript for KeyboardEvent vs MouseEvent when you use those fields.
topics.title: Event object

topics.summary: Use input.value or FormData.
topics.description: Read a single field with input.value (always a string for text controls). For whole forms, new FormData(form) collects named fields. Checkboxes and radios need .checked as well as value. Trim strings before validating or sending.
topics.whenToUse: Gathering user-entered data for display, storage, or requests.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not scrape textContent of the field — use the value property.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that empty inputs are "" not null.
Reading select.value vs selectedOptions incorrectly.
beginnerTips: Give inputs name attributes for FormData and accessibility labels.
Number(input.value) or parseFloat when you need math.
topics.title: Reading input

topics.summary: checkValidity / setCustomValidity / manual checks.
topics.description: Browsers ship constraint validation: required, type, min/max, pattern. call form.checkValidity() or input.reportValidity() to surface native messages. setCustomValidity("msg") adds your own rule (clear with ""). Combine with JS checks for rules HTML cannot express.
topics.whenToUse: Before submit or when guiding users to fix fields.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not rely only on client checks — validate again on the server.
commonMistakes: Disabling validation with novalidate without replacing it.
Only checking on submit and never as the user edits.
beginnerTips: Use input type=email/url/number for free baseline checks.
Keep error messages specific and next to the field.
topics.title: Validating input

topics.summary: Stop the browser’s default action (like navigating on submit).
topics.description: preventDefault() cancels the browser’s built-in response to an event: form navigation, link follow, key scroll in some cases. Call it synchronously in the handler. It does not stop other listeners unless you also stop propagation. Use it when JS will handle the action instead.
topics.whenToUse: Custom submit handlers, in-page links, and drag/drop overrides.
topics.whenNotToUse: When the default behavior is what you want — do not block it.
commonMistakes: Awaiting fetch before preventDefault — too late, page already navigated.
Preventing defaults globally and breaking accessibility.
beginnerTips: Pair with form submit listeners, not only button clicks.
Check event.cancelable if you are unsure a default can be blocked.
topics.title: preventDefault

topics.summary: Update UI as the user types or selects.
topics.description: Wire input/change listeners to keep previews, character counts, and dependent fields in sync. Update only what changed when possible. Debounce expensive work like filtering large lists. Reflect state in the DOM so users get immediate feedback.
topics.whenToUse: Live previews, enabling/disabling buttons, cascading selects.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not hit the network on every keypress without debouncing.
commonMistakes: Updating unrelated parts of the page on each keystroke.
Fighting the user by resetting the cursor while they type.
beginnerTips: Derive UI from a small state object, then render — easier than scattering DOM writes.
Disable submit until required fields are non-empty.
topics.title: Responding to changes

topics.summary: Show text near fields; wire aria-describedby.
topics.description: Show validation errors next to the field that failed, not only in an alert. Connect the message with aria-describedby and set aria-invalid="true" when appropriate. Clear errors when the user fixes the input. Keep wording short and actionable.
topics.whenToUse: Client-side validation feedback and server error mapping.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not rely on color alone — include text.
commonMistakes: Announcing errors only visually for screen-reader users.
Leaving stale error text after the field becomes valid.
beginnerTips: Reuse native reportValidity when it fits your design.
Focus the first invalid field after a failed submit.
topics.title: Displaying errors

topics.summary: Reflect form state into previews and totals.
topics.description: Use form values to recompute totals, toggle sections, and refresh summaries as controls change. Keep a single update function you call from multiple listeners. Prefer textContent for numeric/text previews. Hide optional sections with classes rather than destroying fields you still need on submit.
topics.whenToUse: Calculators, configurators, multi-step forms with live summaries.
topics.whenNotToUse: Static confirmation pages that do not change with input.
commonMistakes: Duplicating calculation logic in several handlers.
Removing inputs from the DOM and losing their values on submit.
beginnerTips: Store money/quantities as numbers in variables, format only for display.
Run one initial update() on page load so the UI matches defaults.
topics.title: Dynamically update content

topics.summary: Add one or more classes.
topics.description: classList.add("name") adds a class if it is not already present. You can pass multiple names in one call. It will not duplicate the class. Pair with CSS rules that define what that class looks like — JS only flips the switch.
topics.whenToUse: Turning on a visual or state class.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not add classes that have no CSS — they only clutter the markup.
commonMistakes: Passing a selector like ".hi" — use the bare class name "hi".
Using add when toggle would express on/off intent better.
beginnerTips: add is idempotent — safe to call even if the class exists.
Keep class names stable; treat them as an API between JS and CSS.
topics.title: classList.add

topics.summary: Remove classes.
topics.description: classList.remove("name") drops a class if present; it is safe when the class is already absent. Remove state classes when closing menus, clearing errors, or resetting themes. Multiple names can be removed in one call.
topics.whenToUse: Clearing a state you previously added.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not remove structural classes your CSS always needs unless you mean to.
commonMistakes: Misspelling the class name and wondering why styles remain.
Clearing className entirely and wiping unrelated classes.
beginnerTips: Mirror every add path with a remove (or use toggle).
remove returns undefined — chain via the classList object if needed.
topics.title: classList.remove

topics.summary: Add if missing, remove if present.
topics.description: toggle switches a class on or off. With one argument it flips state; with a second force boolean it adds when true and removes when false. Perfect for open/closed UI and dark-mode switches driven by one button.
topics.whenToUse: Binary UI states controlled by the same control.
topics.whenNotToUse: When you only ever add or only ever remove — use add/remove for clarity.
commonMistakes: Toggling two competing classes separately and getting both on.
Forgetting to persist theme toggles if users expect them to stick (localStorage).
beginnerTips: const isOn = el.classList.toggle("on") tells you the new state.
force parameter: toggle("open", shouldOpen).
topics.title: classList.toggle

topics.summary: Returns true if the class is present.
topics.description: contains("name") reports whether the class is currently on the element. Use it for branching when CSS alone cannot decide the next action. Prefer toggle’s return value or force flag when you are about to flip state anyway.
topics.whenToUse: Reading current class state before running logic.
topics.whenNotToUse: Styling decisions that CSS can express with the class itself.
commonMistakes: Checking className.indexOf which false-positives on partial names.
Using contains in a tight animation loop instead of events.
beginnerTips: Keep JS checks in sync with the same class names CSS uses.
Avoid duplicating state in a boolean and a class — pick one source of truth.
topics.title: classList.contains

topics.summary: Run a function once after a delay (ms).
topics.description: setTimeout(fn, ms) schedules fn to run once after roughly ms milliseconds and returns an id. Delays are not exact under load. Use it for deferred UI updates, toasts, and timeouts around async work. Store the id if you might cancel with clearTimeout.
topics.whenToUse: One-shot delayed work.
topics.whenNotToUse: Regular repeats — use setInterval or recursive setTimeout with care.
commonMistakes: Calling setTimeout(fn(), ms) which runs fn immediately and schedules its return value.
Creating timers in a loop without clearing them on teardown.
beginnerTips: Pass arguments: setTimeout(fn, ms, arg1).
0 ms still waits until after the current tasks finish.
topics.title: setTimeout

topics.summary: Run repeatedly until cleared.
topics.description: setInterval(fn, ms) calls fn repeatedly every ms until clearInterval. Overlaps can happen if fn takes longer than the delay — consider recursive setTimeout for “wait then run again” timing. Always clear intervals when a component unmounts or a page view ends.
topics.whenToUse: Clocks, polling (sparingly), simple animations.
topics.whenNotToUse: High-frequency animation — prefer requestAnimationFrame.
commonMistakes: Starting a new interval on every click without clearing the old one.
Polling a server too aggressively and hammering the network.
beginnerTips: Save the id: const id = setInterval(...); clear later.
Pause by clearing; restart by creating a new interval.
topics.title: setInterval

topics.summary: Cancel a pending timeout by id.
topics.description: clearTimeout(id) cancels a timeout scheduled by setTimeout so the callback never runs. Harmless if the timeout already fired or the id is invalid. Keep the id in a variable from the moment you schedule it if cancellation is possible (user navigates away, new input supersedes).
topics.whenToUse: Debouncing and canceling deferred work that is no longer needed.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not clear intervals with clearTimeout — use clearInterval.
commonMistakes: Losing the id and being unable to cancel.
Assuming clearTimeout stops a callback that already started running.
beginnerTips: Debounce pattern: clearTimeout then setTimeout on each event.
Null out your stored id after clearing for easier debugging.
topics.title: clearTimeout

topics.summary: Stop a repeating interval.
topics.description: clearInterval(id) stops a setInterval timer. Call it when the repeating work should end: user clicks stop, a condition is met, or the UI is torn down. Without clearing, intervals keep running and can leak memory or fight new code.
topics.whenToUse: Stopping clocks, polls, and repeating tasks.
topics.whenNotToUse: One-shot timeouts — those use clearTimeout.
commonMistakes: Orphan intervals after navigating within a single-page app.
Clearing the wrong id when several timers are active.
beginnerTips: Clear in both success and error paths when polling.
Centralize start/stop helpers so ids do not scatter.
topics.title: clearInterval

topics.summary: JavaScript Object Notation — text format for data.
topics.description: JSON is a text format for structured data used by APIs and storage. It supports objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. It does not allow functions, comments, or trailing commas. Keys must be double-quoted strings. Think of it as a data interchange format, not full JavaScript.
topics.whenToUse: Exchanging data with servers or persisting simple structures as text.
topics.whenNotToUse: Storing executable code or JS-specific types like Date without a convention.
commonMistakes: Writing JS object literals with unquoted keys and calling it JSON.
Including trailing commas that JSON.parse rejects.
beginnerTips: Validate shapes after parsing — JSON only checks syntax.
Prefer arrays of objects for lists of records.
topics.title: JSON structure

topics.summary: Convert a value to a JSON string.
topics.description: JSON.stringify turns a JavaScript value into a JSON text string. Undefined properties, functions, and symbols are omitted (or become null in arrays). Pass a space argument for pretty printing. Use it before localStorage or sending bodies to APIs that expect JSON.
topics.whenToUse: Serializing data for storage or HTTP bodies.
topics.whenNotToUse: Values that contain circular references — stringify throws.
commonMistakes: Assuming undefined fields survive round-trips.
Stringifying twice and ending up with an escaped string blob.
beginnerTips: JSON.stringify(value, null, 2) indents for debugging.
Provide a toJSON method on objects for custom serialization.
topics.title: JSON.stringify

topics.summary: Parse a JSON string into a value.
topics.description: JSON.parse reads a JSON string and returns objects, arrays, or primitives. Invalid JSON throws SyntaxError — wrap in try/catch when the string is from users or the network. After parsing, verify the shape you expect before using deep properties.
topics.whenToUse: Reading API bodies, localStorage payloads, and config files.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not eval JSON as JavaScript — always parse.
commonMistakes: Parsing without try/catch on untrusted text.
Trusting parsed data without checking types/fields.
beginnerTips: response.json() on fetch is parse under the hood.
A reviver function can transform dates during parse.
topics.title: JSON.parse

topics.summary: Use URLSearchParams on location.search.
topics.description: URL query strings carry key/value pairs after ?: ?units=1,2,3&mode=demo. URLSearchParams parses them: get, getAll, has, and iteration helpers. Use new URLSearchParams(location.search) in the browser. Missing keys return null from get — handle defaults explicitly.
topics.whenToUse: Reading shareable state from the address bar (filters, ids, modes).
topics.whenNotToUse: Secrets — query strings end up in logs and history.

files.code:
const params = new URLSearchParams("units=1,2,3&mode=demo");
document.getElementById("o").textContent = params.get("units");

commonMistakes: Manual string splits that break on encoding.
Forgetting decode is already handled by URLSearchParams.
beginnerTips: params.get("id") ?? "default" covers missing values.
new URL(location.href).searchParams is another common pattern.
topics.title: Reading URL parameters

topics.summary: Key/value string storage that persists per origin.
topics.description: localStorage saves string key/value pairs for an origin (scheme + host + port). Data survives refreshes and browser restarts until cleared. The API is synchronous and size-limited (often ~5MB). It is not secure storage — anything script can read, XSS can read.
topics.whenToUse: Remembering preferences, drafts, and light client state.
topics.whenNotToUse: Passwords, tokens you cannot afford to leak, or large binary data.
commonMistakes: Storing sensitive credentials in localStorage.
